title: What happens in the brain when musicians make up music on the spot?
blurb: Scientists at the US National Institutes of Health scanned jazz pianists' brains while they made up tunes. A part of the brain that judges and checks went quiet.

cover.alt: A computer picture of a brain from the side. Orange patches show parts that got busier, and blue and green patches show parts that got quieter.
cover.credit: Figure 3, Limb and Braun, PLOS ONE 2008, public domain (CC0)

source.name: PLOS ONE (research paper)
source.title: Neural Substrates of Spontaneous Musical Performance: An fMRI Study of Jazz Improvisation
source.authors: Charles J. Limb, Allen R. Braun

original.title: Neural Substrates of Spontaneous Musical Performance: An fMRI Study of Jazz Improvisation
original.authors: Limb, C. J., and Braun, A. R.

cards.b: When musicians make up music while they play, it is called improvising. Jazz musicians do it all the time. Jazz is a kind of music from the United States. Carnatic musicians improvise too, in parts of a concert where they invent as they sing. How does a brain invent new music so fast? Which parts of the brain get busier, and which go quiet?

Charles Limb is a doctor who studies hearing, and he also plays jazz. Allen Braun studies the brain and language. They worked at the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders, part of the US National Institutes of Health. Charles Limb also worked at Johns Hopkins University. They published in 2008.

Six professional jazz pianists lay inside a brain scanner, a big machine that shows which brain parts are working hardest. It uses a giant magnet, so they played a special plastic keyboard with no metal. First they played a tune they had learned by heart. Then they made up their own music over the same backing band. The scientists compared the two.

img.alt: A small piano keyboard at the top, and below it lines of written music: tunes learned by heart on the left, and made-up tunes on the right.
img.credit: Figure 1, Limb and Braun, PLOS ONE 2008, public domain (CC0)

cards.b: When the pianists made up music, a large area at the sides of the front of the brain went quiet. This area helps us check ourselves and stop mistakes. At the same time, a small area in the middle front got busier. This area is linked to expressing who we are. Parts that control fingers and hearing got busier too.

img.alt: Slices of a brain seen from above, with blue patches where the brain went quieter and orange patches where it got busier during made-up music.
img.credit: Figure 2, Limb and Braun, PLOS ONE 2008, public domain (CC0)

cards.b: Only six musicians took part, all men and all right-handed. That is a small group, so the results need checking with more people. The same pattern showed up in two different tests, which makes it more believable. Scientists still do not fully understand how creativity works in the brain.

The scientists noticed something interesting. A similar pattern, with the self-checking area quiet, has been seen during dreaming. In dreams, ideas flow without us checking them. Making up music may work a little like that. Knowing this helps scientists study creativity, the making of new ideas and new things, in art, science and play.

Play a made-up music game with a steel plate and a spoon. One person taps a simple beat. The other person copies it exactly, like the pianists playing a tune they knew. Then the other person makes up their own beat in reply, without stopping to plan, like the pianists improvising. Which felt easier? Which felt more fun? Swap turns and try again.

To make up music, the pianists' brains seemed to switch off some self-checking. But checking helps us avoid mistakes. Is it good to stop worrying about mistakes when we create something? Or do we need some checking to make it good? When do you feel most free to invent?

words.m: to make something up on the spot, without planning it first
a big machine that shows which parts of the brain are working hardest
the ability to make new ideas or new things
a kind of music from the United States where players often make up parts as they go
